native_verses.14:2: And I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for war, and the city will be captured, the houses will be ransacked, and the women will be violated; and half of the city will go out into exile, but the remainder of the people will not be cut off from the city.
native_verses.14:3: Then the LORD will go out and fight against those nations, as on the day of His fighting on a day of battle.
native_verses.14:4: And His feet will stand on that day on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split down its center eastward and westward into a very great valley, and half of the mountain will move northward and half of it southward.
native_verses.14:5: And you will flee by the valley of My mountains, for the valley of the mountains will reach to Azal; and you will flee just as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with You.
native_verses.14:6: And it will happen on that day that there will be no light, bright splendors, or freezing.
native_verses.14:7: And it will be a single day, which is known to the LORD, not day and not night; and it will happen that at evening time there will be light.
native_verses.14:8: And it will happen on that day that living water will flow out from Jerusalem, half of it to the eastern sea and half of it to the western sea; in summer and in winter it will happen.
native_verses.14:9: And the LORD will become king over the whole earth; on that day the LORD will be one, and His name will be one.
native_verses.14:10: The entire land will be turned into a plain, from Geba to Rimmon, south of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem will rise high and remain in its place, from the Gate of Benjamin to the site of the First Gate, to the Corner Gate, and from the Tower of Hananel to the winepresses of the king.
native_verses.14:11: And people will dwell in it, and there will never again be a ban of destruction, and Jerusalem will dwell in safety.
native_verses.14:12: And this will be the plague by which the LORD will strike all the peoples who marched to war against Jerusalem: their flesh will decay while they stand on their feet, their eyes will decay in their sockets, and their tongues will decay in their mouths.
native_verses.14:13: And it will happen on that day that a great panic from the LORD will be among them, and each man will seize the hand of his companion, and his hand will rise up against the hand of his companion.
native_verses.14:14: And Judah too will fight at Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the nations all around will be gathered up, gold and silver and clothing in very great abundance.
native_verses.14:15: And likewise will be the plague on the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey, and all the livestock that will be in those camps, just like this plague.
native_verses.14:16: And it will happen that everyone left from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year after year to bow down to the King, the LORD of hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Booths.
native_verses.14:17: And it will happen that whichever of the families of the earth does not go up to Jerusalem to bow down to the King, the LORD of hosts, on them there will be no rain.
native_verses.14:18: And if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come, then on them there will be none; there will be the plague by which the LORD will strike the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Booths.
native_verses.14:19: This will be the penalty of Egypt, and the penalty of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Booths.
native_verses.14:20: On that day there will be on the bells of the horses, "Holy to the LORD." And the pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar.
native_verses.14:21: And every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the LORD of hosts, and all who sacrifice will come and take from them and boil in them. And there will never again be a merchant in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day.

native_notes.1:4: The ketiv reads a longer orthographic form with an extra yod (um'alileikhem); the qere reads uma'alleleikhem ("and your deeds"), the regular plural of ma'alal with a 2mp suffix, which is translated here.
native_notes.1:8: Hebrew metsulah normally refers to a depth (often of water) and here designates a low-lying hollow or glen; seruqqim ("sorrel") occurs only here as a horse color and denotes a reddish-brown or chestnut hue.
native_notes.1:15: Literally "they helped for evil/calamity" (azeru lera'ah), an idiom meaning that the nations exceeded God's intended discipline and intensified Judah's disaster.
native_notes.1:16: The ketiv reads the older spelling qaweh (cf. 1 Kgs 7:23; Jer 31:39); the qere reads the standard form qaw ("a measuring line"), which is translated here.
native_notes.2:4: The clause kefi-ish lo-nasa rosho is idiomatic (literally "according to the measure that no man raised his head"); leyaddot ("to cast down") is the Piel infinitive construct of yadah II ("throw/cast").
native_notes.2:10: The interjection hoy (doubled here and repeated in 2:11) functions as an urgent summons to attention and flight rather than a lament; the preposition ke literally means "like" ("like the four winds of the heavens").
native_notes.2:12: The elliptical phrase achar kavod literally means "after glory" (variously understood as "for the sake of glory," "in pursuit of glory," or "after the glory"). The hapax legomenon bavah ("pupil") denotes the delicate center of the eye; Masoretic tradition lists eino ("His eye") among the scribal emendations (Tiqqune Sopherim) for "My eye," and the speaker alternates between the sent messenger (here and at the ends of 2:13, 2:15) and the LORD.
native_notes.2:17: The verb ne'or is the Niphal perfect of ur ("to awake/rouse oneself"), portraying the LORD stirring Himself to act from His heavenly dwelling.
native_notes.3:1: Hebrew ha-satan ("the Accuser" or "the Adversary") carries the definite article as a courtroom title and forms a cognate wordplay with the Qal infinitive construct lesitno ("to accuse him").
native_notes.3:4: Hebrew wehalbesh is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of labash ("to clothe/dress") continuing the preceding finite verb he'evarti (Hiphil perfect of avar, literally "I have caused to pass away"); machalatsot denotes costly or festive robes (elsewhere only in Isa 3:22).
native_notes.3:7: The rare form mahlekim is variously parsed as the plural of mahalak ("walkways/rights of access") or an Aramaizing Hiphil participle of halak ("ones who walk"), granting Joshua access among the heavenly attendants.
native_notes.3:8: Hebrew tsemach ("Branch" or "Sprout") lacks the definite article and functions here as a title or proper name (cf. 6:12).
native_notes.4:2: Translated from the Qere וָאֹמַר ("and I said," 1cs); the Ketiv reads ויאמר ("and he said," 3ms). The distributive phrase שִׁבְעָה וְשִׁבְעָה מוּצָקוֹת ("seven and seven pipes") likely denotes seven pipes for each of the seven lamps, or fourteen pipes in total.
native_notes.4:7: הָאֶבֶן הָרֹאשָׁה uses the rare feminine form רֹאשָׁה (from רֹאשׁ, "head/first/top"), literally "the stone, the head/chief one," referring either to the crowning capstone that completes the temple or to its premier stone.
native_notes.4:10: הָאֶבֶן הַבְּדִיל is literally "the stone, the tin," denoting a tin plumb weight or plummet (or a ceremonial metal stone). Following the Masoretic accentuation, שִׁבְעָה־אֵלֶּה ("these seven") serves as the subject of וְשָׂמְחוּ וְרָאוּ ("will rejoice when they see").
native_notes.4:12: צַנְתְּרוֹת is a biblical hapax legomenon denoting conduits or pipes, and הַזָּהָב is literally "the gold," referring poetically to golden olive oil.
native_notes.4:14: בְּנֵי־הַיִּצְהָר is literally "sons of the fresh oil," a Hebrew idiom for figures consecrated with or characterized by fresh olive oil, commonly understood as anointed ones.
native_notes.5:3: מִזֶּה ... מִזֶּה idiomatically means "on one side ... on the other side" (the two sides of the scroll), כָּמוֹהָ ("according to it") refers to the curse, and Niphal נִקָּה (from נקה) carries the sense "be purged/cleaned out" (cf. Isa 3:26) rather than "be acquitted."
native_notes.5:6: הָאֵיפָה ("the ephah") is a dry measuring vessel of roughly 22 liters. Masoretic עֵינָם (lit. "their eye") is used idiomatically for "their appearance/aspect" (cf. Lev 13:55; Num 11:7), whereas the Septuagint and Syriac reflect a variant Hebrew reading עֲוֹנָם ("their iniquity").
native_notes.5:11: וְהוּכַן (Hophal of כּוּן) is masculine singular, referring to the בַיִת ("house"), whereas וְהֻנִּיחָה (Hophal of נוּחַ) and מְכֻנָתָהּ ("its base/pedestal," also from כּוּן) are feminine singular, referring to the ephah.
native_notes.6:3: אֲמֻצִּים (also in 6:7) derives from the root אמץ ("be strong") yet follows the Hebrew color-adjective pattern (like אֲדֻמִּים "red" and בְּרֻדִּים "dappled"), leading some scholars to understand it as a horse color such as "bay" or "sorrel."
native_notes.6:5: Hebrew רוּחוֹת can mean either "winds" (matching the four compass directions, cf. Zech 2:6) or "spirits" (matching their standing in the heavenly court before God, cf. Ps 104:4).
native_notes.6:12: צֶמַח ("Branch") and יִצְמָח ("will branch out") play on the root צמח, literally "sprout/shoot" and "sprout up"; מִתַּחְתָּיו is literally "from beneath him," an idiom for "from his own place."
native_notes.6:13: וְהָיָה כֹהֵן עַל־כִּסְאוֹ is syntactically ambiguous in Hebrew and may be read either as "a priest will be on his throne" (a second figure beside the royal Branch, matching "between the two of them") or as "he will be a priest on his throne" (uniting royal and priestly roles in one figure).
native_notes.6:14: Plural הָעֲטָרֹת ("the crowns," as in 6:11) takes a feminine singular verb תִּהְיֶה, indicating either a single composite crown or collective crowns. חֵלֶם ("Helem") and חֵן ("Hen," also possibly the common noun "graciousness") correspond to Heldai and Josiah in 6:10.
native_notes.7:2: In the Masoretic accentuation, Bethel is the subject ("Bethel sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and his men"), though some construe Bethel-sharezer as a single Babylonian personal name or read Bethel as the destination. The idiom translated "implore the favor of" literally means "appease/soften the face of" (Piel of chalah).
native_notes.7:7: The Hebrew begins with the interrogative particle and direct-object marker (halo et-haddevarim) without an expressed verb, implying a verb such as "hear" or "heed"; alternatively, et may function as an emphatic subject marker ("Are these not the words...").
native_notes.7:14: The Hebrew verb rendered "I scattered them as in a storm" is an unusual imperfect form from sa'ar ("whirl/storm away"), used here in context for the past exile that left the land desolate.
native_notes.8:6: The Niphal verb (yippale, from pala) denotes what is extraordinary, marvelous, or beyond human ability, and the second clause functions as an unmarked rhetorical question.
native_notes.8:12: The opening clause literally reads "for a sowing/seed of peace" without an expressed verb, introducing the threefold promise of agricultural abundance.
native_notes.8:17: The Hebrew combines the direct-object marker (et) with the relative pronoun (asher) before "I hate" (ki et-kol-elleh asher saneti), an emphatic Late Biblical Hebrew construction.
native_notes.9:1: The Masoretic Hebrew literally reads "for to/toward the LORD is the eye of mankind and all the tribes of Israel," indicating either that humanity and Israel look toward the LORD or that His watchful attention encompasses them.
native_notes.9:8: The Hebrew mitstsava (a rare form related to matstsava, "garrison/guard") is rendered "as a guard"; some revocalize it as min-tsava ("against an army/host").
native_notes.9:9: The word rendered "victorious" is a Niphal participle (nosha, from yasha), literally "saved" or "delivered," indicating that the king is granted deliverance and victory by God.
native_notes.9:15: Following the Masoretic Hebrew literally ("sling stones" and "as with wine"); the closing simile evokes the mizraq, the temple basin used for dashing sacrificial blood onto the corners of the altar.
native_notes.9:17: The third-person masculine singular suffixes on "goodness" and "beauty" may refer to the LORD (compare Jeremiah 31:12, where the LORD's goodness yields grain and new wine) or collectively to His people in verse 16.
native_notes.10:3: Hebrew uses the same verb paqad in two opposite senses: with the preposition al ("call to account" or "punish") and with the direct object marker et ("attend to" or "care for"). "Male goats" (attudim) is a Hebrew metaphor for flock leaders.
native_notes.10:4: Hebrew uses the masculine singular pronoun mimmennu ("from it" or "from him"), referring collectively to the house of Judah in v. 3. The Qal participle noges normally means "taskmaster" or "oppressor," but here denotes an authoritative commander or ruler.
native_notes.10:6: The verb wehoshbotim is a rare mixed Hebrew form blending the Hiphil of yashav ("settle" or "cause to dwell") and the Hiphil of shuv ("bring back" or "restore," cf. v. 10).
native_notes.10:11: Hebrew bayyam tsarah literally reads "through the sea, affliction," an appositional construction meaning "the sea of affliction" or "distress." The third-person masculine singular verbs ("He will pass... strike") have the LORD as subject.
native_notes.11:2: Ketiv reads habbatsur (Qal passive participle of batsar, "fortified" or "inaccessible"), while Qere reads the adjective habbatsir ("impenetrable" or "dense"); both describe a thick, impenetrable forest.
native_notes.11:7: Following the Masoretic Text laken aniyye hattson ("indeed, the afflicted of the flock"; cf. v. 11). The Septuagint redivides the consonants to read "for the sheep merchants."
native_notes.11:13: The Masoretic Text clearly reads hayyotser (Qal participle of yatsar, "the potter"). Some ancient versions (e.g. the Syriac) reflect ha'otsar ("the treasury") instead.
native_notes.11:16: Hebrew hanna'ar normally means "the young" (collectively, the young of the flock). Some interpreters instead connect the word to the verb na'ar ("shake out") and render it "the scattered" or "straying."
native_notes.11:17: The final -i on ro'i ("shepherd") and ozevi ("who deserts") is the archaic poetic linking vowel (hireq compaginis) rather than the first-person possessive suffix "my."
native_notes.12:2: The Hebrew clause literally reads "and also upon Judah it will be in the siege against Jerusalem," which may mean either that Judah too will be caught in the siege or that Judah will be forced into the siege against Jerusalem.
native_notes.12:5: Hebrew allufe ("chiefs" or "leaders"; also in v. 6) can alternatively be rendered "clans." The singular pronoun li ("to me") is distributive, representing each leader's inner thought.
native_notes.12:10: The Masoretic Text reads elay ("to Me") with et asher-daqaru ("whom they have pierced") and then shifts to the third-person pronoun alav ("over Him"). The form wehamer is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of marar ("grieve bitterly") continuing the preceding finite verb.
native_notes.12:11: The construct phrase "mourning of Hadad-rimmon" may refer either to lamentation at a place named Hadad-rimmon (often linked to King Josiah's death, 2 Chr 35:22-25) or to ritual mourning for a deity of that name. Hebrew spells Megiddo here as Megiddon.
native_notes.13:5: Hebrew hiqnani is a unique Hiphil perfect of qanah ("acquire, buy"), here understood causatively as "sold me" (transferred ownership of me), though some render it "acquired me" or "made me possess [land]."
native_notes.13:6: Hebrew ben yadekha literally means "between your hands," an idiom likely referring to the chest or upper back; me'ahavay is a Piel participle of ahav ("those who love me").
native_notes.13:8: Hebrew pi-shenayim literally means "a portion of two," here denoting two-thirds in contrast to hashelishit ("the third part").
native_notes.14:2: Ketiv reads tishshagalnah (Niphal imperfect of shagal, a coarser verb for sexual assault); Qere substitutes the euphemistic Niphal imperfect tishshakhavnah (from shakhav, "be lain with," i.e., "be violated").
native_notes.14:5: MT reads wenastem ("and you will flee," Qal perfect of nus) twice, matching nastem ("you fled"); ancient versions such as the Septuagint read a Niphal of satam ("will be blocked"). Note also the abrupt person shifts in MT from "My mountains" (the LORD speaking) to "my God" and "with You" (the prophet addressing the LORD).
native_notes.14:6: A difficult Hebrew text: MT reads yeqarot ("bright/precious things," likely celestial lights, cf. Job 31:26) followed by Qere weqippa'on ("and/or freezing/congealing," a noun from qafa'); Ketiv reads the Qal imperfect verb yiqpa'un ("they will congeal/dwindle").
native_notes.14:18: MT places the major disjunctive accent on welo alehem ("and not on them"), elliptically echoing "no rain" from v. 17 since Egypt relied on the Nile rather than rain; some read welo as a rhetorical question ("will not the plague be on them?").
native_notes.14:21: Hebrew kena'ani literally means "Canaanite," but is also used idiomatically in Biblical Hebrew for "merchant" or "trader" (cf. Prov 31:24), fitting the temple-vessel context of vv. 20-21.
